Loving the Unlovable.
You know, we all have those parts of ourselves we wish we could just hide away—the angry moments, the jealous thoughts, those little flashes of weakness or shame. Maybe you’ve caught yourself thinking, “If I could just get rid of these flaws, then maybe I’d finally feel accepted.” But here’s something powerful: real wholeness doesn’t come from being perfect. It comes from embracing every single part of who you are. Think about a middle-aged man—he’s haunted by memories of a tough divorce, carrying around this heavy sense of guilt. He replays old arguments in his head, convinced he’s just not worthy of love. For years, he tries to bury those memories, but they keep bubbling up—especially when he’s feeling lonely or lost. Then one day, while he’s out for a quiet walk, he stops. He imagines holding his younger self—the version of him that made mistakes, lashed out in pain. Gently, he whispers words of forgiveness. He lets himself feel the sadness and longing beneath all that anger. And in that moment, he realizes something big: even the parts he wants to push away are simply longing for a little compassion. Most of us don’t realize it, but the pieces we work hardest to hide—they’re usually the ones crying out for love the most. When you turn toward those “unlovable” places with a bit of kindness, something inside starts to soften. The walls of shame begin to crumble, and a real sense of wholeness starts to emerge. Here’s another example: a teacher, constantly struggling with impatience in her classroom. She notices how often she’s hard on herself for losing her temper. One afternoon, after snapping at a student, she pauses. She brings gentle attention to the shame she feels in her chest. She remembers what it was like as a kid—the pressure to be perfect, the fear of messing up. So, she offers herself the same understanding she’d give a friend. The next day, she apologizes to her student—not out of guilt, but from a place of real care. So, loving the unlovable isn’t about excusing bad behavior or ignoring how your actions affect others. It’s about seeing the pain underneath, and giving it the compassion it needs to heal. Over time, this practice brings something truly freeing—the permission to be fully human, with all your flaws and all your gifts.
